history.hpi: 34-year-old male reports sudden onset of rapid, irregular palpitations approximately 25 minutes ago while at rest, associated with lightheadedness and mild left-sided chest discomfort. Denies loss of consciousness. States he has had similar brief episodes in the past that resolved on their own, but this one has not stopped. No recent illness, no drug use reported.
pastMedical: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (diagnosed at age 19, never ablated)
history.lastOralIntake: Lunch approximately 3 hours ago; black coffee 1 hour ago
history.events: Onset of rapid irregular heartbeat and lightheadedness while watching television; wife called 911 when it did not resolve after 20 minutes

scene.dispatch: 34-year-old male, palpitations and dizziness, patient conscious and breathing, residence.
scene.location: Single-family home, living room; patient seated on couch
scene.safety: No scene hazards identified; patient cooperative
scene.bystanders: Wife present, states patient has a history of 'a heart rhythm thing since he was a teenager' and has had short episodes before that 'always went away on their own'
visualCues: Patient appears anxious, hand on chest
Half-empty energy drink can on coffee table
Patient's pulse visibly rapid and irregular at the wrist

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Patient is alert and oriented, seated upright, reporting palpitations, mild dizziness, and mild left-sided chest discomfort for the past 25 minutes. Radial pulse is rapid and irregularly irregular. Monitor shows a wide-complex, irregular tachycardia. Blood pressure is on the low end of normal but the patient is not yet showing signs of severe hypoperfusion.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Mildly tachypneic, lungs clear bilaterally, no accessory muscle use
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse rapid, irregularly irregular; skin cool and slightly diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "My heart is racing and it feels like it's skipping all over the place. I feel a little dizzy but I'm not gonna pass out."

expectedActions.shortAction: Manage airway as necessary; airway patent, no intervention required
expectedActions.rationale: Airway is patent and patient is talking; confirm and monitor.

expectedActions.shortAction: Administer oxygen titrated to target SpO2 94-98% (currently 96%)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer oxygen as appropriate with a target of achieving 94–98% saturation

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate cardiac monitoring and acquire 12-lead EKG
Check blood glucose (98 mg/dL, normal); rules out hypoglycemia as cause
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Check blood glucose and treat hypoglycemia per the Hypoglycemia Guideline
expectedActions.rationale: Hypoglycemia is a listed reversible cause of tachydysrhythmia; glucose here is normal so no dextrose is indicated per the Hypoglycemia Guideline inclusion criteria (BG <60 mg/dL with symptoms).

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize irregularly irregular wide-complex tachycardia as pre-excited AFib (WPW); note short PR interval/delta wave on 12-lead
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: A wide-complex irregular rhythm should be considered pre-excited A-FIB; extreme care must be taken in these patients Characteristic EKG findings include a short PR interval and, in some cases, a delta wave

expectedActions.shortAction: Do NOT give adenosine, diltiazem, verapamil, metoprolol, or digoxin — AV nodal blockers contraindicated in pre-excited AFib
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Avoid AV nodal blocking agents such as adenosine, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, and possibly beta-blockers in patients with pre-excitation A-FIB (e.g., Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome, Lown-Ganong-Levine Syndrome) because these drugs may cause a paradoxical increase in the ventricular response

transitions.if: Procainamide given, AV nodal blockers avoided
transitions.condition: Crew correctly identifies irregular wide-complex tachycardia as pre-excited AFib (WPW) and avoids AV nodal blocking agents, instead initiating procainamide per the stable irregular wide complex tachycardia pathway.
Crew mistakenly administers an AV nodal blocking agent (e.g., adenosine, diltiazem, metoprolol) to the pre-excited AFib rhythm, unmasking exclusive accessory pathway conduction.
Treatment is delayed beyond several minutes without intervention; patient progresses to hemodynamic instability (hypotension, altered mental status) requiring synchronized cardioversion.

phases.name: Procainamide given
phases.description: Crew correctly withholds AV nodal blocking agents and initiates a procainamide infusion for the stable, irregularly irregular wide-complex tachycardia (pre-excited AFib). Over several minutes the ventricular response slows and the patient's symptoms and perfusion improve.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew recognized the irregular wide-complex tachycardia as pre-excited AFib (WPW) and, per protocol, avoided AV nodal blocking agents in favor of procainamide.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Improving, RR trending down toward normal
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse still irregular but slower and stronger; skin warming, less diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Okay, that's better, my chest doesn't feel as tight now."

expectedActions.shortAction: Procainamide 20-50 mg/min IV infusion (86 kg × 17 mg/kg = 1,462 mg maximum total dose); titrate to arrhythmia suppression, hypotension, or QRS widening >50%
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Procainamide 20–50 mg/min until arrhythmia suppressed, hypotension ensues, QRS duration increases greater than 50%, or maximum dose 17 mg/kg given Maintenance infusion: 1–4 mg/min Avoid if prolonged QT or CHF

expectedActions.shortAction: If arrhythmia persists and a second agent is needed, give procainamide before amiodarone (WPW-specific sequencing)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patients with Wolff–Parkinson–White should be given procainamide prior to amiodarone

expectedActions.shortAction: Obtain repeat monitor strip/12-lead after the procainamide infusion to document response
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Obtain monitor strips after each intervention

transitions.condition: Ventricular response slows, symptoms and perfusion improve; patient is prepared for transport with continuous monitoring.

phases.name: Rate controlled, patient stabilized
phases.description: Ventricular response has slowed and perfusion has normalized following procainamide. Patient remains in a pre-excited rhythm (WPW baseline pattern) but is hemodynamically stable and comfortable. Continuous monitoring is maintained for transport to a facility with cardiology capability.
phases.triggerCondition: Procainamide infusion controlled the ventricular rate and improved perfusion; no further antidysrhythmic needed at this time.

clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I feel a lot better now, thanks."

expectedActions.shortAction: Document initial rhythm, all rhythm changes, and time/dose/response to procainamide for handoff
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Initial rhythm and all rhythm changes Time, dose, and response to medications given

phases.name: AV nodal blocker given
phases.description: An AV nodal blocking agent was administered to the pre-excited AFib rhythm. AV node blockade forces conduction exclusively down the accessory pathway, producing a paradoxical increase in ventricular rate. The rhythm rapidly degenerates into ventricular fibrillation and the patient becomes pulseless.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew administered an AV nodal blocking agent (e.g., adenosine, diltiazem, metoprolol) to the irregularly irregular wide-complex tachycardia instead of recognizing it as pre-excited AFib (WPW).

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but unprotected, requires airway management
otherFindings: Sudden collapse seconds after medication administration

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize degeneration into ventricular fibrillation; begin immediate chest compressions and prepare to defibrillate
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Initiate chest compressions in cases with no bystander chest compressions or take over compressions from bystanders while a second rescuer is setting up the AED or defibrillator If adequate, uninterrupted bystander CPR has been performed or if the patient arrests in front of the EMS clinicians, immediately proceed with rhythm analysis and defibrillation, if appropriate

expectedActions.shortAction: Defibrillate at manufacturer's recommended biphasic energy (or highest setting if unknown)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Defibrillation dosing should follow manufacturer's recommendation in the case of biphasic defibrillators. If the manufacturer's recommendation is unknown, use highest setting possible.

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize AV nodal blockade of pre-excited AFib as the precipitating cause of VF
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Blocking the AV node in some of these patients may lead to impulses that are transmitted exclusively down the accessory pathway, which can result in ventricular fibrillation

phases.name: Treatment delayed, patient decompensates
phases.description: Treatment was delayed and the patient has progressed to hemodynamic instability: worsening hypotension and altered mental status. This now meets criteria for the unstable irregular wide-complex tachycardia pathway and requires synchronized cardioversion.
phases.triggerCondition: Antidysrhythmic treatment was not initiated in a timely manner; patient decompensated to hypotension and altered mental status, meeting criteria for unstable tachycardia.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, protecting airway but sluggish responses
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse thready, irregularly irregular, barely palpable; only central pulses palpable
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Normal but slow to follow commands
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I... don't feel right..." (slurred, slow to respond)

expectedActions.shortAction: Deliver synchronized cardioversion per manufacturer's recommended energy settings
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Deliver a synchronized shock based on manufacturer's recommendation

expectedActions.shortAction: Consider sedation and analgesia prior to cardioversion since patient remains responsive
